column9: stem
column14: option_a
column15: option_b
column16: option_c
column17: option_d
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: On a line graph, which axis does the **independent variable** go on?
column14: The y-axis (vertical)
column15: The x-axis (horizontal)
column16: Either axis works the same
column17: It goes in the title, not on an axis
column28: The IV goes on the x-axis (horizontal). The DV goes on the y-axis (vertical).
column29: The IV is the variable you change. Step 1 of building a line graph in your graphing notes says which axis gets it.

column9: Which type of graph is best for showing **percents** of a whole?
column14: Pie chart
column15: Line graph
column16: Histogram
column17: Scatter plot
column28: A pie chart shows percents: each slice is part of the whole 100%.
column29: Which graph is a circle cut into slices that add up to 100%?

column9: Which type of graph is used most often in science?
column14: Pie chart
column15: Bar chart
column16: Line graph
column17: Histogram
column28: Most scientific graphs are line graphs, because they show how the DV changes as the IV changes. Other types are used for special cases.
column29: Think of graphs that show how something changes over time or as the IV goes up.

column9: A graph that plots each pair of IV and DV values as a separate point, with no line or bars drawn, to look for a pattern between two variables, is called a ___ plot.
column28: A scatter plot places each (IV, DV) pair as its own point and leaves the points unconnected, so you can look for a pattern between two number variables. Line graphs have a line through the points, and bar charts and histograms use bars. (A dot plot from math class is different: it stacks dots over a number line for just one variable.)
column29: Think of the graph types in your notes: line graph, bar chart, histogram, pie chart, and one more.

column9: Which graph shows continuous data with **no gaps** between the bars?
column14: Bar chart
column15: Pie chart
column16: Line graph
column17: Histogram
column28: A histogram shows continuous data in ranges, so the bars touch (no gaps). A bar chart compares separate groups, so it has gaps between bars.
column29: Which bar graph has bars that touch?

column9: Match each type of graph to what it is used for.
column14: Line graph :: Shows how the DV changes as the IV changes, like over time
column15: Bar chart :: Compares separate groups, with gaps between the bars
column16: Histogram :: Shows continuous data in ranges, with no gaps between bars
column17: Pie chart :: Shows percents of a whole
column18: Scatter plot :: Shows separate data points to look for a pattern
column28: Line graph = change in the DV as the IV changes. Bar chart = compare groups (gaps). Histogram = continuous ranges (no gaps). Pie chart = percents. Scatter plot = individual points showing a pattern.
column29: Think about the shape of each graph: line, bars with gaps, bars touching, circle, dots.

column9: In a data table, where should the independent variable go?
column14: In the right column
column15: In the title only
column16: In the left column
column17: In a row at the bottom
column28: From the graphing notes: the IV goes on the left side of a data table, and the DV goes on the right side. (On a graph, the IV goes on the x-axis and the DV on the y-axis.)
column29: The IV is what you changed. A table is read left to right, so which variable should a reader see first?

column9: What does a graph need when it shows more than one set of data?
column14: A key
column15: Two titles
column16: A second x-axis
column17: A larger grid
column28: A graph with more than one data set (like two lines) needs a key (legend) so the reader knows which line is which. One title covers the whole graph, both data sets share the same x-axis, and the same grid works as long as the scale fits all of the data.
column29: How would a reader tell the tomato line from the bean line?

column9: What kind of line do most science line graphs use?
column14: A connect-the-dots line
column15: A dotted line
column16: No line at all
column17: A best-fit line
column28: Science line graphs use a smooth best-fit line (straight or curved) that gets close to most of the points. They are usually not drawn connect-the-dots.
column29: Real measurements never land perfectly on a smooth pattern. Should the line chase every point that is a little off?

column9: In a CER, what is the **claim**?
column14: The data tables and graphs from the lab
column15: A one-sentence answer to the problem statement
column16: The science reason the evidence supports the answer
column17: A list of possible experimental errors
column28: The claim is your answer to the problem statement in one sentence. Data tables and graphs are the evidence, the science reason is the reasoning, and errors go in the reflection.
column29: C is for claim. What does the claim answer?

column9: In the **evidence writing** part of a CER, how many statements should you summarize your data into to describe the trends and patterns? ___
column28: The class CER template asks you to summarize your data into 3 statements that describe the trends and patterns. That keeps the evidence concise: the reader gets the main results without rereading the whole data table.
column29: Evidence writing turns a whole data table into a short list of summary sentences. Check the Evidence writing step of the CER template.

column9: You record your heart rate four times after drinking Mountain Dew: 86, 83, 88, and 85 beats per minute. What is the mean heart rate? (Do not round.)
column28: Mean = sum ÷ number of values = (86 + 83 + 88 + 85) ÷ 4 = 342 ÷ 4 = 85.5 beats per minute.
column29: Add all four values, then divide by how many there are.

column9: What does **directly proportional** mean on a graph?
column14: As the IV increases, the DV decreases.
column15: As the IV increases, the DV increases too.
column16: The DV stays the same no matter what.
column17: The IV and DV are the same variable.
column28: Directly proportional: as the IV increases, the DV increases (the line goes up). Inversely proportional: as the IV increases, the DV decreases (the line goes down).
column29: Think of a case you know, like more fertilizer giving taller plants. What happens to each variable as the first one goes up?

column9: When you choose a scale for a graph, it is best to use only a small part of the grid so there is room to spare.
column28: False. Choose a scale that fits all of your data and uses most of the graph, so the pattern is big and easy to see. A graph squeezed into one corner hides the trend.
column29: Would a pattern be easier to see on a big graph or on a tiny one squeezed into a corner?

column9: Labeling a graph's x-axis "Time" is complete; the units are not needed.
column28: False. Every axis needs a label AND units, like "Time (days)." Without units, a reader can't tell if it means seconds, days, or months.
column29: Could "Time" mean seconds or weeks?

column9: Mr. E surveys Cadott students about the truck brand they own: Chevrolet 25, Ford 14, Ram 9, GMC 6. Which graph is best for comparing the brands?
column14: Line graph
column15: Histogram
column16: Scatter plot
column17: Bar chart
column28: The brands are separate groups (categories), so a bar chart with gaps between the bars is best for comparing them. A line graph would suggest change over time, and a histogram needs number ranges.
column29: Are the truck brands separate categories or a range of numbers?

column9: A DNR worker measures 20 brook trout and counts how many fall into each length range: 10–14 cm, 15–19 cm, 20–24 cm, and 25–29 cm. Which graph should she make?
column14: Histogram
column15: Pie chart
column16: Bar chart
column17: Line graph
column28: Length is continuous data grouped into ranges, so a histogram (bars touching, no gaps) is best. A bar chart is for separate categories, like trout species.
column29: The ranges run into each other with no gaps between them. Which graph has touching bars?

column9: Ella asks all 20 students in her class to name their one favorite type of music: country 8, pop 6, rock 4, rap 2. She wants to show what share of the whole class chose each type. Which graph should she make?
column14: Line graph
column15: Histogram
column16: Pie chart
column17: Bar chart
column28: Every student picked exactly one type, so the four counts make up the whole class: country 8 of 20 = 40%, pop 30%, rock 20%, rap 10%. To show each type's share of the whole, use a pie chart: each slice is part of the whole class. A bar chart would compare the counts side by side, but it doesn't show each type as a part of one whole. A histogram is for number ranges, and a line graph shows how the DV changes as the IV changes.
column29: Add the four counts. What do they add up to, and what does Ella want a reader to see?

column9: Kaylee gave bean plants 0, 5, 10, or 15 g of fertilizer and measured their height in cm. Which is the best graph title?
column14: Height of Bean Plants in Centimeters
column15: Plant Height vs. Amount of Fertilizer
column16: My Bean Plant Experiment Graph
column17: Plant Height vs. Number of Days
column28: A good title clearly tells what the graph is about by naming both variables: what was changed (fertilizer, the IV) and what was measured (height, the DV). A common format is DV vs. IV. "Plant Height vs. Number of Days" uses that format but names the wrong IV: Kaylee changed the amount of fertilizer, not the time. "Height of Bean Plants in Centimeters" leaves out the fertilizer, and "My Bean Plant Experiment Graph" doesn't name either variable.
column29: A good title clearly tells what the graph is about. What did Kaylee change, and what did she measure?

column9: Ty counted how many times a goldfish's gill covers opened per minute at different water temperatures. How should he set up his graph?
column14: x-axis: Gill openings per minute; y-axis: Water temperature (°C)
column15: x-axis: Water temperature; y-axis: Gill openings (no units needed)
column16: x-axis: Goldfish; y-axis: Water temperature and gill openings
column17: x-axis: Water temperature (°C); y-axis: Gill openings per minute
column28: Ty changed the temperature (IV, x-axis) and counted gill openings (DV, y-axis). Each axis needs a label with units. Swapping the axes or leaving off units makes the graph incomplete.
column29: IV on the x-axis, DV on the y-axis, and units on both.

column9: Goldfish data table. Temperature (°C): 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 | Gill openings per minute: 22, 34, 47, 61, 40. By how many openings per minute did the rate increase from 10 °C to 25 °C?
column28: At 10 °C the rate was 22 and at 25 °C it was 61. Increase = 61 − 22 = 39 openings per minute.
column29: Find the value under 10 °C and the value under 25 °C, then subtract.

column9: Students find that as the amount of road salt in the soil increases, the height of the grass decreases. What is this relationship?
column14: Directly proportional
column15: No relationship
column16: Inversely proportional
column17: Extrapolated
column28: As the IV (road salt) increases, the DV (grass height) decreases, so the relationship is inversely proportional. On a graph, the line slopes down.
column29: Does the DV go up or down as the IV goes up?

column9: A bean plant was 3.6 cm tall on Day 2 and 5.9 cm tall on Day 4. Using a graph of these data to estimate its height on Day 3 is called...
column14: Interpolating
column15: Extrapolating
column16: Hypothesizing
column17: Observing
column28: Interpolating is predicting data between two measured points (Day 3 is between Days 2 and 4). Extrapolating is extending the graph beyond the measured data.
column29: Is Day 3 between your data points or beyond them?

column9: Grace counted how many times a cricket chirped per minute at 15, 20, 25, and 30 °C. She uses her graph to predict the chirps per minute at 10 °C. What is this called, and why?
column14: Extrapolating, because 10 °C is outside the range she measured
column15: Interpolating, because 10 °C is close to her lowest temperature
column16: Interpolating, because she is predicting backward, not forward
column17: Averaging, because she uses all of her measured data to predict
column28: Extrapolating means predicting outside the range of measured data, in either direction. 10 °C is below her lowest temperature (15 °C), so this is extrapolating, even though it comes before her data instead of after it. Being close to the data or predicting "backward" doesn't make it interpolating, and averaging gives one typical value, not a prediction at a new temperature.
column29: Is 10 °C between two of the temperatures she tested, or outside them?

column9: Five radish seeds took 3, 4, 4, 5, and 6 days to sprout. What is the mean number of days? (Do not round.)
column29: Add the five values, then divide by 5.

column9: Problem: "Does the amount of light affect how tall bean plants grow?" Which is the best **evidence** statement?
column14: The plants with more light seemed to do a lot better than the other plants did.
column15: Plants with 8 hours of light grew to a mean of 14 cm; plants with 2 hours grew to 4 cm.
column16: Light helps plants grow because plants need light energy to make their food.
column17: We think the amount of light probably matters for how tall bean plants get.
column28: Good evidence uses specific data (numbers with units) from the experiment. "Seemed to do better" is vague, the light-energy sentence is reasoning, and "we think" is a guess, not evidence.
column29: Evidence is what you measured, not what you think or why it happened. Which sentence could you check against the data table?

column9: Problem: "Does water temperature affect how fast yeast makes gas?" Which is the best **claim**?
column14: At 40 °C the balloon grew 12 cm, but at 10 °C it grew 2 cm.
column15: Warm water speeds up the chemical reactions in yeast cells.
column16: Next time we should test more temperatures and bottles.
column17: Yeast makes gas faster in warmer water.
column28: The claim is a one-sentence answer to the problem. The balloon measurements are evidence, the chemical reaction sentence is reasoning, and testing more temperatures belongs in the reflection.
column29: Which sentence directly answers the problem statement in one sentence?

column9: Put the steps for constructing a line graph in order, as taught in class.
column14: Draw a best-fit line or curve
column15: Plot the data points
column16: Determine the scale for each axis
column17: Title the graph
column18: Identify the independent and dependent variables
column19: Number and label each axis with units
column28: From the class notes: (1) identify the variables, (2) determine the scale, (3) number and label each axis with units, (4) plot the data points, (5) draw the best-fit line, (6) title the graph (and add a key if there is more than one data set).
column29: You can't choose a scale until you know which variable goes on each axis, and you can't draw a line until the points are plotted.

column9: Kaylee's y-axis has 10 squares. Her bean plant heights range from 0 mm (day 0) to 90 mm. Which scale fits all the data and uses most of the graph?
column14: 10 mm per square
column15: 1 mm per square
column16: 20 mm per square
column17: 100 mm per square
column28: With 10 mm per square, 90 mm lands on the 9th square: everything fits and most of the space is used. 1 mm per square only reaches 10 mm, 20 mm per square leaves about half the graph empty, and 100 mm per square squashes all the data into one square.
column29: Divide the biggest value by the number of squares, then round up to an easy number.

column9: Which things does every complete data table need? Select all that apply.
column14: Variable names as column headings
column15: Lines drawn with a straight edge
column16: Units for each variable
column17: The hypothesis written above the table
column28: A complete data table has a descriptive title, the variables as column headings, (units) for each variable, and lines drawn with a straight edge. The hypothesis goes in its own part of the lab write-up, not on the table, and a key is something you add to a graph, not to a data table.
column29: A data table only organizes your measurements. Which choices help a reader understand the numbers, and which belong somewhere else in a lab report or on a graph?

column9: Problem: "Does exercise affect heart rate?" Which sentence belongs in the **Reasoning** section of the CER?
column14: After jumping jacks, our mean heart rate rose from 72 to 118 beats per minute.
column15: Exercise makes a person's heart beat faster than it does at rest.
column16: Working muscles need more oxygen, so the heart pumps faster to deliver it.
column17: We may have miscounted some pulses; next time we would use a heart monitor.
column28: Reasoning explains WHY the evidence supports the claim, using science ideas (working muscles need oxygen, and the heart delivers it). The heart-rate numbers are evidence, the one-sentence answer to the problem is the claim, and the miscounted pulses belong in the reflection.
column29: Which sentence explains why it happens, using a science idea instead of data?

column9: Hailey tested whether the amount of water affects how tall pea plants grow. Which is a real **experimental error** she should list in her reflection?
column14: Her results did not match the hypothesis she wrote before the lab.
column15: She used ten pea plants in each group instead of only one plant.
column16: The pea plants that got more water grew taller than the others.
column17: She accidentally gave one of her pots extra water on day 3.
column28: An experimental error is a mistake in how the experiment was done that could change the data, like giving one pot extra water. Results that don't match the hypothesis are not an error; a hypothesis that isn't supported is still a useful result. Using ten plants per group is good design (more trials), and "plants with more water grew taller" is a result for the claim and evidence.
column29: An error is a mistake in HOW the experiment was done. Which one could have changed the data?

column9: In a lab like the Thumb Lab, Jacob ties his shoe in 8 s using his thumbs and in 20 s with his thumbs taped. Use: % difference = (no-thumb time − thumb time) ÷ thumb time × 100. What is the % difference?
column29: Subtract first, divide by the thumb time, then multiply by 100.

column9: Data table. Hours of light per day: 2, 4, 6, 8 | Plant height (cm): 5, 9, 14, 18. Which statement describes the trend?
column14: As hours of light increase, plant height decreases.
column15: As hours of light increase, plant height increases.
column16: Plant height stays about the same no matter how much light the plants get.
column17: Plant height increases at first, then decreases as light increases.
column28: Height goes up (5, 9, 14, 18 cm) as light goes up (2 to 8 hours), so the DV increases with the IV: directly proportional. Height never goes down in this data, so "increases, then decreases" is a misreading.
column29: As you read the light row left to right, what happens to the height row?

column9: Drew planted 40 radish seeds and 30 of them sprouted. What percent of the seeds sprouted?
column29: Divide the part by the whole, then multiply by 100.

column9: At a nature center, Ava counts the frog egg masses in four ponds. On the trail map, the ponds are numbered Pond 2, Pond 5, Pond 9, and Pond 14. Which graph should she use to show her data, and why?
column14: A line graph, because the pond numbers go up in order, from Pond 2 to Pond 14
column15: A histogram, because pond numbers are continuous data that can be put in ranges
column16: A bar chart, because each pond is a separate category, even though it is numbered
column17: A scatter plot, because the pond numbers and egg mass counts are both numbers
column28: The IV is which pond, and the pond numbers are only names (labels) on the map. Pond 9 is not "more pond" than Pond 5, and nothing sits halfway between Pond 2 and Pond 5. Separate categories go on a bar chart, with gaps between the bars. A line graph or a scatter plot would treat the pond numbers as a number scale, and a histogram is for measured, continuous data (like lengths) grouped into ranges.
column29: Do the pond numbers measure an amount of something, the way temperature or days do, or do they just name each pond?

column9: Jace's graph has "Plant height (cm)" on the x-axis, "Time (days)" on the y-axis, and the title "Graph." Which fixes does it need?
column14: Keep the axes, but add a key and change the title to "Plant Graph"
column15: Remove the units from both axes and make it a bar chart instead
column16: Keep everything the same, but connect every dot with straight lines
column17: Swap the axes so time is on the x-axis, and write a descriptive title
column28: Time is the IV, so it belongs on the x-axis, and height (DV) goes on the y-axis. The title should clearly tell what the graph is about, like "Plant Height vs. Time." A key is only needed for more than one data set, and units must stay.
column29: Which variable is the IV? And does "Graph" tell the reader anything?

column9: Maya timed four trials of a pill bug crossing a 20 cm track. Her mean time was 12.75 s. Three of the trials were 12.4 s, 13.0 s, and 12.7 s. What was the fourth trial, in seconds?
column28: Mean = total ÷ number of trials, so total = mean × number of trials = 12.75 × 4 = 51.0 s. The three known trials add to 12.4 + 13.0 + 12.7 = 38.1 s. Fourth trial = 51.0 − 38.1 = 12.9 s. Check: (12.4 + 13.0 + 12.7 + 12.9) ÷ 4 = 51.0 ÷ 4 = 12.75 s.
column29: Work backward: the mean is the total ÷ 4. What must the total of all four trials be?

column9: Data: mean brine shrimp eggs hatched (out of 50) at different amounts of salt per 100 mL of water. 0 g: 5; 2 g: 22; 4 g: 41; 6 g: 18. Which evidence-writing statement best summarizes a pattern in the data?
column14: Hatching kept rising as more salt was added, from 0 g up to 6 g.
column15: Hatching rose from 5 to 41 as salt rose to 4 g, then fell to 18 at 6 g.
column16: Salt is important to brine shrimp because they live in salty lakes.
column17: Some eggs hatched and some didn't, so the results were kind of mixed.
column28: Good evidence writing uses specific numbers to describe trends and patterns. The data rise and then fall, so "kept rising" is wrong. The salty lake sentence is reasoning, and "kind of mixed" is too vague.
column29: Check each statement against the actual numbers. Do the numbers only go up?

column9: Hypothesis: "If water temperature increases, then brine shrimp eggs will hatch faster." Mean hatch time at 15 °C: 48 h; 20 °C: 36 h; 25 °C: 30 h; 30 °C: 40 h. Which conclusion is best?
column14: Partly supported: hatching sped up to 25 °C, then slowed at 30 °C.
column15: Fully supported, because the eggs at 25 °C hatched faster than the eggs at 15 °C.
column16: Refuted, because the eggs at 30 °C took longer to hatch than the eggs at 20 °C.
column17: Cannot be judged at all, because hatch times are not a good thing to measure.
column28: Hatch time dropped (faster hatching) from 48 h to 30 h as temperature rose to 25 °C, then rose to 40 h at 30 °C. The data support the hypothesis only up to 25 °C. A good conclusion describes the whole pattern, not just two data points.
column29: Look at all four temperatures. Does hatching get faster every single time?

column9: On a goldfish graph, the best-fit line is straight. At 10 °C the fish took 20 breaths per minute, and at 20 °C it took 40 breaths per minute. Use the line to estimate about how many breaths per minute the fish would take at 16 °C.
column28: From 10 °C to 20 °C the breaths go up by 20, so each 1 °C adds 2 breaths per minute. 16 °C is 6 °C above 10 °C: 20 + 6 × 2 = 32 breaths per minute. Because 16 °C is between two measured points, this is interpolating.
column29: On a straight line, equal steps in temperature give equal steps in breaths. How many extra breaths does each 1 °C add?

column9: Kaylee's graph shows bean plants grew taller as the temperature rose from 10 °C to 30 °C. She extends her line to predict that the plants would be even taller at 60 °C. Which statement about her prediction is best?
column14: It is reliable, because the line went up the whole way from 10 °C to 30 °C.
column15: It is reliable, as long as she draws the best-fit line carefully with a ruler.
column16: It is risky, because the trend may not continue; that much heat could kill plants.
column17: It is risky, but only because her x-axis would have to be made longer.
column28: Extrapolating assumes the pattern keeps going beyond the measured data. 60 °C is far past her highest temperature (30 °C), and heat that extreme would likely harm or kill the plants, so the trend may not continue. A line that rose the whole way, or one drawn neatly with a ruler, still only shows what happened from 10 °C to 30 °C. Making the axis longer is easy; the real problem is that nobody measured what happens at 60 °C.
column29: Would a bean plant really keep getting taller if it were kept at 60 °C, hotter than any summer day?

column9: Kaylee measured the heights of tomato, bean, and corn plants every day for 7 days. What is the best way to graph all of her data?
column14: Three pie charts, one for each type of plant, showing the percent of growth
column15: One bar chart with plant type on the y-axis and days on the x-axis
column16: One multiple line graph of height vs. days, one line for each plant type
column17: One histogram with all of the heights grouped together into ranges
column28: Each plant's height changes over time (days), so line graphs fit. Putting all three lines on one multiple line graph (same variables and units) makes them easy to compare, and because it shows more than one data set it needs a key so the reader knows which line is which. Pie charts show percents of a whole, not change over time. The bar chart puts plant type and days on the axes, so height (the DV) has nowhere to go. One histogram of all the heights mixes the three plants together and loses the days.
column29: All three data sets share the same IV and DV. How can one graph show all three, clearly?

column9: Data: percent of seeds that sprouted at different amounts of salt per 100 mL of water. 0 g: 95%; 2 g: 80%; 4 g: 50%; 6 g: 10%. Which statements are supported by the data? Select all that apply.
column14: At 4 g of salt, half of the seeds sprouted
column15: At 8 g of salt, exactly 0% of the seeds will sprout
column16: As salt increased, the percent of seeds that sprouted decreased
column17: The independent variable is the percent of seeds that sprouted
column28: Sprouting fell from 95% to 10% as salt went up, which is inversely proportional, and 50% is half. The data are about how many seeds sprouted, not how fast. Salt is the IV, not the percent. 8 g was not tested, so "exactly 0%" is an extrapolation, not a fact.
column29: For each statement, find the numbers in the data that prove it. If you can't point to them, don't pick it.

column9: Ella's data for how far mealworms crawled in 1 minute range from 5 cm to 75 cm. She numbered her y-axis 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 60, 80, with one number on each grid line. What is the problem?
column14: The axis should start at 5 cm, her smallest value, instead of at 0.
column15: The jumps between the numbers are not all the same size.
column16: The axis goes up to 80 cm, which is past her largest value.
column17: Nothing is wrong, because all of her data fit on the axis.
column28: Her jumps are 10, 10, 10, 10, 20, 20, so the grid squares don't all stand for the same amount. Each square must stand for the same amount, or the shape of the data gets distorted (values above 40 cm would look squashed). Starting at 0 is fine, ending a little above the largest value is fine, and fitting all the data isn't enough if the spacing is unequal.
column29: Find the difference between each pair of neighboring numbers on the axis.

column9: Heart rates after drinking Dr. Pepper: 81, 84, 79, 82 beats per minute. After drinking water: 72, 70, 75, 71 beats per minute. How many beats per minute higher is the Dr. Pepper mean than the water mean? (Do not round the means.)
column29: Find each mean separately, then subtract the smaller from the larger.

column9: Match each sentence from Aliya's lab write-up to the part of the CER template where it belongs.
column14: "Does water temperature affect how fast radish seeds sprout?" :: Problem Statement
column15: "Radish seeds sprout faster in warmer water." :: Claim
column16: "At 25 °C, seeds sprouted in 2 days, but at 10 °C they took 6 days." :: Evidence
column17: "Warmth speeds up the chemical reactions in the seeds, so they can grow sooner." :: Reasoning
column18: "We may have miscounted sprouts; next time we would test more seeds." :: Reflection
column28: The problem statement is the question. The claim answers it in one sentence. The evidence gives the data. The reasoning explains why the evidence supports the claim. The reflection names errors and next experiments.
column29: Go through the CER template one part at a time. Say in your own words what job that part does, then find the sentence that does that job.

column9: Students recorded how many times crickets chirp per minute at different temperatures. Which data table setup is correct?
column14: Title: Cricket Chirps vs. Temperature. Left: Temperature (°C). Right: Chirps per minute.
column15: Title: Cricket Chirps vs. Temperature. Left: Chirps per minute. Right: Temperature (°C).
column16: Title: Cricket Chirps vs. Temperature. Left: Temperature (°C). Right: Chirps.
column17: Title: Cricket Data. Left: Temperature (°C). Right: Chirps per minute.
column28: A complete table has a descriptive title that names the variables, the IV (temperature) in the left column and the DV (chirps per minute) in the right column, and units for each variable. Putting chirps on the left swaps the IV and DV. A column headed only "Chirps" leaves out the time unit: chirps per second? per minute? per hour? The title "Cricket Data" doesn't tell what was changed or what was measured.
column29: Check every part against the data table rules: the title, which variable is on the left, and the units in each column heading.

column9: Liam ran one trial: his fertilized radish plants grew 2 cm **less** than his unfertilized ones. Mia ran the same test five times, and her fertilized plants grew a mean of 3 cm **more**. Whose result is better evidence about fertilizer, and why?
column14: Liam's, because a single trial is a real measurement, not a calculated number.
column15: Liam's, because the first trial of an experiment is usually the most careful one.

column17: Mia's, because one unusual trial has less effect on the mean of five trials.
